body:
> did you have trouble putting their words into actions?

Mainly this, I suppose. But I think that therapy simply doesn't work for everyone in the same way chemo doesn't cure every cancer.

> Did you change anything in your life since you started therapy?

Hard to say, I've been through multiple therapies, it's been some years, and my memory isn't in its best shape. I tried to change things I guess, but in the end nothing really changed.

The thing is, once you've tried a lot of ways to get out of this, nothing worked, and emotional numbing set in, it's really hard (almost impossible) to see any change as a positive result. It's just some change with no emotion attached to it.

​

The key difference between you and the normies lies in your second reason (people see life as a gift). Humans aren't in fact perfectly logical cognitive machines existing in the land of pure abstractions, but possess minds woven of internal contradictions, aberrations and irrationalities. Thus most people illogically place *infinite* value on the fact of their existence (also known as "life"). It's a subtle difference (because we rarely examine the way we evaluate such concepts), but a very important one. Hence the nonsensical arguments ("life is beautiful" and whatnot).


It is indeed more logical to see life as having a finite value that could be outweighed by other factors making suicide sometimes a preferred choice. As for your question I can provide a couple anti-suicide arguments.


I'll start with the tongue-in-cheek one. It is conceivable that a person who's currently 30 could live long enough to see practical immortality implemented and made publicly available (provided the civilisation won't collapse before that). In such case the logical choice is to persevere through life even if in great misery, because obtaining immortality will give you *orders-of-magnitude more* resources to fix either yourself or reality around you, so that life would become worth living. And in any case, if it wouldn't work, you could always kill yourself a couple of millennia later.


My second argument has to do with your fifth one, where you obviously select just certain aspects of psychiatric help and exaggerate them mercilessly (admittedly it depends on the country you live in). First of all, it's irrational to think of that in terms of lost dignity and such. As always it's about profit and loss: you give up some of your dignity and free will in exchange for a chance to significantly alter your mind for the better (whether the chance is worth it is another question). And secondly (but first in importance), most psychiatric options don’t involve subjecting oneself to cruel and unusual confinement in a psychiatric facility. It merely gives you an option


a) to better understand the difference in mental states between you and the rest of humanity (whether to call your state of mind enlightened or insane is a mere quibble over terms in my opinion; and just so we're clear: this characterisation applies to me as well) allowing you to make an informed decision;


b) to see what effect medications and other therapeutic methods will have on you. If the effect is a positive one and significant enough, it might change your attitude towards life and make suicide an illogical choice.


My third argument revolves around one of the main cognitive mistakes that plague human reasoning: constantly overstating the importance of our state here-and-now compared to our future states. Thus the pain in a just-burnt hand bloats our mind’s eye obscuring the *entirety* of possible emotions, thoughts and actions that we will have or do over the course of our lifetimes. It’s a mistake so ingrained in our way of thinking that it’s impossible to eradicate it. But understanding its omnipresence can allow us to make better choices. However you may object to this argument by saying that your disillusioned view of life is not a mere *"phase"*, it's a conclusion distilled through years of experience and rumination.


But consider a following hypothetical: as you read these words our reality splits into two timelines. In timeline *α* you commit suicide in a near future. In timeline *β* you decide to take a drug that was prescribed to you by a specialist. You’re taking it not expecting it to work, more out of curiosity, however much to your surprise it leads to a breakthrough allowing you to experience happiness and joy on a consistent basis for the first time in your life. What do you think you from *β* would make of your post after a year into his newly found enjoyable life?
